books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution, Section 2 (ratified 1868)

stimulus.text:
“Representatives shall be apportioned among the several States according to their respective numbers, counting the whole number of persons in each State, excluding Indians not taxed. But when the right to vote at any election for the choice of electors for President and Vice-President of the United States, Representatives in Congress, the Executive and Judicial officers of a State, or the members of the Legislature thereof, is denied to any of the male inhabitants of such State, being twenty-one years of age, and citizens of the United States, or in any way abridged, except for participation in rebellion, or other crime, the basis of representation therein shall be reduced...”

—Fourteenth Amendment, Section 2, ratified 1868
stimulus.source_note: Fourteenth Amendment, Section 2, ratified 1868. Public domain. Wording verified against the Constitution Annotated (Congress.gov). Trailing ellipsis marks omitted text.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The word “male” in this section mattered because it was

options.text: the first time the Constitution used the word “male.”
a ban on women ever voting in any state.
options.misconception: Background: the section does not ban women from voting; it ties representation to male voters, which is why suffragists objected to it.

options.text: the first mention of slavery in the Constitution.
options.misconception: Background: slavery first appears by name in the Thirteenth Amendment, not here.

options.text: a grant of the vote to all women.
options.misconception: Background: the section mentions no grant of the vote to anyone, let alone to women.

rationales.A: Before this amendment, the Constitution never used “male” or “female,” so suffragists could argue that nothing in it barred women from voting. Section 2 tied the vote to male inhabitants, writing women out of the Constitution’s voting language for the first time.
rationales.B: Background: the section does not ban women from voting; it ties representation to male voters, which is why suffragists objected to it.
rationales.C: Background: slavery first appears by name in the Thirteenth Amendment, not here.
rationales.D: Background: the section mentions no grant of the vote to anyone, let alone to women.
rationales.general:
1. The section ties representation to “the male inhabitants” of a state.
2. Background: before 1868, the Constitution never said “male” or “female” at all.
3. Suffragists had argued that silence left the door open for women.
4. One word closed it, and the women’s movement split over the loss.
Remember: a single new word can change what a whole document allows.
